title: Multimedia
overview: Images and sound must be turned into binary before a computer can store them. Paper 1 asks you to explain how bitmaps and vector graphics are encoded, calculate bitmap and sound file sizes, describe how changing resolution, colour depth, sampling rate or sampling resolution affects quality and size, and justify choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic for a given task.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of how data for a bitmapped image are encoded, using the terms pixel, file header, image resolution, screen resolution, colour depth and bit depth.
Perform calculations to estimate the file size for a bitmap image.
Show understanding of the effects of changing elements of a bitmap image on the image quality and file size.
Show understanding of how data for a vector graphic are encoded, using the terms drawing object, property and drawing list.
Justify the use of a bitmap image or a vector graphic for a given task.
Show understanding of how sound is represented and encoded, using the terms sampling, sampling rate, sampling resolution, analogue data and digital data.
Show understanding of the impact of changing the sampling rate and resolution, and calculate the file size of a sound file.

definitions.definition: The smallest addressable element of a bitmap image; a single dot of one colour.
The number of pixels in an image, given as width × height (for example 1920 × 1080).
The number of pixels a display screen can show horizontally and vertically.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of one pixel; n bits allow 2^n different colours.
The number of bits used to store each of the red, green and blue components of a pixel's colour; a bit depth of 8 gives 24 bits per pixel.
Data at the start of an image or sound file describing the file, such as its type, dimensions, colour depth or sampling rate.
A single shape in a vector graphic, such as a line, rectangle or circle.
A value that defines how a drawing object looks, such as its coordinates, size, line colour, line width or fill colour.
The set of commands in a vector graphic file that define every drawing object and its properties.
The number of samples of a sound wave's amplitude taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The number of bits used to store each sound sample; it sets how many amplitude levels can be recorded.

sections.title: Encoding bitmap images
content: A bitmap image is a two-dimensional grid (matrix) of pixels. A pixel has just two properties: its position in the grid and its colour. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary code, and the codes are stored in order, row by row. The number of bits per pixel is the colour depth: 1 bit gives 2 colours (black and white), 4 bits allow simple greyscale, 8 bits give 256 colours and 24 bits give over 16.7 million colours. Bit depth is the number of bits for each of the red, green and blue components, so a bit depth of 8 means 3 × 8 = 24 bits per pixel. A high colour depth is needed for areas of gradually changing colour, such as a sky; with too few bits the image shows visible bands of colour. A file header at the start of the file records information the software needs to rebuild the image, such as the file type, image width and height, and colour depth.
bullets: Image resolution is a property of the image (how many pixels it contains); screen resolution is a property of the display.
If the image resolution is higher than the screen resolution, the image is scaled down or only part of it is shown.
Enlarging a bitmap beyond its resolution makes the individual pixels visible (pixelation).

examples.label: Colours available from a colour depth
examples.content:
Colour depth 4 bits → 2^4 = 16 colours
Colour depth 8 bits → 2^8 = 256 colours
Colour depth 24 bits → 2^24 = 16,777,216 colours

sections.title: Calculating bitmap file size
content: The pixel data in a bitmap take up (number of pixels) × (colour depth) bits. Multiply the width by the height to find the number of pixels, multiply by the colour depth, then divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes. The result is an estimate, because the file header adds a small amount of extra data.
bullets: Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KiB or by 1000 for kB, depending on the unit the question asks for.
Keep the calculation in one line of working so method marks can be awarded.
State that the file header makes the real file slightly larger than the estimate.

examples.label: File size of a 1024 × 768 image with 16-bit colour
Using bit depth instead of colour depth
examples.content:
An 800 × 600 image has a bit depth of 8 (per RGB component).
Bits per pixel = 3 × 8 = 24, i.e. 3 bytes
Size = 800 × 600 × 3 = 1,440,000 bytes ≈ 1406.3 KiB

examples.label: Size of a scanned photo from dpi
examples.content:
A 6 × 4 inch photo is scanned at 300 dots (pixels) per inch with 24-bit colour.
Pixels = (6 × 300) × (4 × 300) = 1800 × 1200 = 2,160,000
Bytes = 2,160,000 × 3 = 6,480,000 bytes
= 6,480,000 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 6.2 MiB

sections.title: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
content: Increasing the image resolution gives more pixels, so finer detail can be shown and the image can be enlarged further before pixelation appears. Increasing the colour depth allows more colours, so shades and gradients look more realistic with less colour banding. Both changes increase the file size in direct proportion: doubling the colour depth doubles the size, and doubling both the width and the height quadruples it.
bullets: Reducing resolution or colour depth reduces file size but lowers quality; this is a trade-off, not a free saving.
A larger file takes longer to download or transmit and uses more storage.
Always link a change to both effects the question asks for: quality and file size.

examples.label: Predicting the new file size
examples.content:
An image is 2 MiB. Its width and height are both halved and its colour depth is changed from 24 bits to 8 bits.
Pixels fall to ½ × ½ = ¼ of the original
Bits per pixel fall to 8 ÷ 24 = ⅓ of the original
New size = 2 MiB × ¼ × ⅓ ≈ 0.17 MiB

sections.title: Encoding vector graphics
content: A vector graphic does not store pixels. Instead it stores a drawing list: a set of commands describing each drawing object and its properties, such as a circle's centre coordinates, radius, line colour, line width and fill colour. Dimensions are defined relative to an imaginary drawing canvas rather than in fixed units. When the image is displayed, the software reads the drawing list and recalculates every object at the required scale, so the graphic can be resized without losing quality or being distorted. Vector graphics are produced by drawing and computer-aided design (CAD) packages. Most screens and printers work with pixels, so a vector graphic is converted to a bitmap (rasterised) at the moment it is displayed or printed.
bullets: File size depends on the number and complexity of objects, not on the display size.
Scaling only changes property values, so edges stay sharp at any size.
Vector graphics are poor at representing photographs, because natural scenes cannot be broken down into simple shapes.

examples.label: A drawing list entry
examples.content:
Circle: centre (120, 80), radius 40, line colour black, line width 2, fill colour red
Rectangle: top-left (20, 20), width 60, height 30, line colour blue, fill none

sections.title: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
content: Choose a bitmap when the image has continuous tones and fine, irregular detail, such as a photograph or a scanned document. Choose a vector graphic when the image is built from lines and shapes and must be resized, such as a logo, a diagram, a map, a font or a technical drawing. In a justification, name the feature of the task and link it to a property of the format.
bullets: Logo printed on a pen and on a billboard → vector, because it must scale without pixelation.
Photograph from a digital camera → bitmap, because each pixel's colour can be captured individually.
Simple diagrams are often smaller as vectors; complex photographs would need a vast drawing list.
Useful questions to decide: Must the image be resized? Must it be drawn accurately to scale (e.g. an architect's plan)? Must it look photo-realistic?
Images captured by a digital camera or scanner are always bitmaps.

sections.title: Sampling sound
content: Sound is an analogue wave: its amplitude varies continuously over time. To store it digitally, a sound encoder first passes the signal through a band-limiting filter, which removes very high frequencies that humans cannot hear and that would cause coding problems. An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) then measures (samples) the amplitude at regular time intervals, and each measurement is rounded to the nearest level that can be stored with the sampling resolution. These binary sample values are stored in order, with a file header recording details such as the sampling rate and sampling resolution. Played back, the samples are converted into an approximation of the original wave.
bullets: Analogue data vary continuously; digital data take discrete values.
The sampling rate controls how often the wave is measured; the sampling resolution controls how precisely each measurement is stored.
A sampling resolution of n bits gives 2^n possible amplitude levels, e.g. 3 bits gives only 8 levels, while 16 bits gives 65,536.
Nyquist's theorem: the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the sound. Human hearing reaches about 20 kHz, which is why CDs sample at 44.1 kHz with 16-bit resolution.

sections.title: Sound quality and file size
content: A higher sampling rate captures changes in the wave more often, so rapid changes (higher frequencies) are represented and the playback is closer to the original. A higher sampling resolution rounds each sample less, so the amplitude is recorded more accurately with less quantisation error. Both improve accuracy but increase the file size: file size = sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds (× number of channels).
bullets: Doubling the sampling rate or the sampling resolution doubles the file size.
Stereo sound has two channels, so it needs twice the data of mono.
Beyond a certain point, extra quality cannot be heard, so a larger file brings no practical benefit.

examples.label: File size of a 30-second stereo recording
examples.content:
Sampling rate = 44,100 Hz, sampling resolution = 16 bits, 2 channels, 30 seconds
Bits = 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 30 = 42,336,000 bits
Bytes = 42,336,000 ÷ 8 = 5,292,000 bytes
MiB = 5,292,000 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 5.05 MiB

formulas.label: Bitmap file size
formulas.expression: size in bits = width (pixels) × height (pixels) × colour depth (bits)

formulas.label: Sound file size
formulas.expression: size in bits = sampling rate (Hz) × sampling resolution (bits) × duration (s) × channels

formulas.label: Converting units
formulas.expression: bytes = bits ÷ 8; KiB = bytes ÷ 1024; MiB = KiB ÷ 1024

comparisonTable.title: Bitmap images and vector graphics
rows: A drawing list of objects and their properties
Individual objects can be moved or resized

diagram.title: Digitising a sound
nodes: Measure amplitude at regular intervals (sampling rate)
Round each sample to a level (sampling resolution)
Store samples as binary with a file header
Play back as an approximation of the wave

analysisChains.title: Increasing the colour depth of a bitmap
steps: Each pixel is stored with more bits
More colours can be represented, e.g. 256 to 16.7 million
Gradients and skin tones look smoother and more realistic
But the file size rises in proportion, so it takes more storage and longer to transmit
analysisChains.evaluation: A high colour depth is worth it for photographs; for a two-colour icon or line drawing it only wastes space.

analysisChains.title: Increasing the sampling rate of a recording
steps: Samples are taken more often each second
Faster changes in the wave are captured
The digital sound is a more accurate copy of the analogue original
But the file size rises in proportion to the sampling rate
analysisChains.evaluation: Music needs a high sampling rate to sound faithful; speech for a voice call can use a much lower rate, saving bandwidth with little loss of clarity.

analysisChains.title: Using a vector graphic for a company logo
steps: The logo is stored as shapes and their properties
It can be scaled for a business card or a large banner
Edges stay sharp because each object is recalculated at the new size
The file stays small because it holds a short drawing list
analysisChains.evaluation: Vectors suit logos and diagrams, but a photographic background in the logo would need to be a bitmap.

examTips: In file-size calculations, write the full expression with units before calculating, and state the final unit clearly.
Check whether the question wants bits, bytes, KiB or MiB, and whether to use 1024 or 1000.
When describing a change (e.g. higher resolution), give its effect on both quality and file size.
For 'justify bitmap or vector' questions, tie the answer to the specific task (scaling, photographic detail, editing).
Use the exact syllabus terms: drawing object, property, drawing list, sampling rate, sampling resolution.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by 8 to convert a size in bits into bytes.
Treating a bit depth of 8 as 8 bits per pixel; bit depth is per RGB component, so it is 24 bits per pixel.
Confusing image resolution (pixels in the image) with screen resolution (pixels on the display).
Saying vector graphics are made of pixels, or that bitmaps store shapes.
Confusing sampling rate (how often) with sampling resolution (how many bits per sample).
Forgetting to multiply by 2 for a stereo recording.
Claiming that raising quality settings has no cost; every increase also increases file size.

quickRecall.question: What is colour depth?
quickRecall.answer: The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel.

quickRecall.question: How many colours can a 12-bit colour depth represent?
How do you estimate the file size of a bitmap?
quickRecall.answer: Width × height × colour depth gives bits; divide by 8 for bytes.

quickRecall.question: What does a vector graphic's drawing list contain?
quickRecall.answer: Commands defining each drawing object and its properties, such as coordinates, size and colours.

quickRecall.question: Why does a vector graphic not pixelate when enlarged?
quickRecall.answer: Each object is recalculated from its properties at the new size rather than stretching stored pixels.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between sampling rate and sampling resolution?
quickRecall.answer: Sampling rate is how many samples are taken per second; sampling resolution is how many bits store each sample.

quickRecall.question: What is the formula for the size of a sound file?
quickRecall.answer: Sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds × number of channels (in bits).

quickRecall.question: What does Nyquist's theorem say about the sampling rate?
quickRecall.answer: It must be at least twice the highest frequency in the sound being sampled.

quickRecall.question: What does a file header store?
quickRecall.answer: Information about the file needed to decode it, such as file type, dimensions and colour depth, or sampling rate and resolution.
